java-sqli-statement-concat.problem: Building a SQL query by concatenating strings with a variable embeds that variable directly into the query text sent to the database.
java-sqli-statement-concat.impact: An attacker who controls any part of that variable can read, modify, or delete arbitrary data — full SQL injection, often leading to total database compromise.
java-sqli-statement-concat.fix: Use a PreparedStatement with ? placeholders and pass parameters via setString / setInt / setLong. Never concatenate user input into a query string.

java-sqli-prepared-concat.problem: Using prepareStatement defeats its own purpose when the SQL string is built by concatenation — the placeholder mechanism is bypassed because the variable is already baked into the SQL text.
java-sqli-prepared-concat.impact: Same as a raw Statement: SQL injection with full read/write access to the database.
java-sqli-prepared-concat.fix: Put ? in the SQL string for every variable and bind values with setString/setInt. Example: prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?") then ps.setInt(1, id).

java-deserialization-readobject.problem: ObjectInputStream.readObject() rebuilds arbitrary Java objects from a byte stream. If the stream comes from an untrusted source, attackers can craft payloads that execute code during deserialization via gadget chains.
java-deserialization-readobject.impact: Remote code execution on the JVM running the deserialization — typical entry point for many high-severity Java CVEs.
java-deserialization-readobject.fix: Avoid Java serialization for untrusted data — prefer JSON with a strict schema. If you must use it, install a serial filter via ObjectInputFilter (Java 9+) or jdk.serialFilter.

java-xxe-documentbuilder.problem: DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance() returns a parser that, by default, resolves external DTDs and entities. A malicious XML document can reference local files, internal URLs, or cause denial of service.
java-xxe-documentbuilder.impact: XML External Entity (XXE): file disclosure, server-side request forgery, denial of service.
java-xxe-documentbuilder.fix: Disable dangerous features right after newInstance(): setFeature(XMLConstants.FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING, true), setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true), setXIncludeAware(false), setExpandEntityReferences(false).

java-runtime-exec-user-input.problem: Runtime.getRuntime().exec called with a variable command runs whatever ends up in that variable. If any part is user-controlled, the attacker decides what process runs.
java-runtime-exec-user-input.impact: Arbitrary command execution on the server — full RCE.
java-runtime-exec-user-input.fix: Never build the command from user input. If the command itself is fixed, use the array form exec(new String[]{"cmd", arg1, arg2}) so arguments are not parsed by a shell. Prefer ProcessBuilder with a hard-coded executable and validated arguments.

java-weak-crypto-md5.problem: MD5 has known practical collisions and is no longer considered safe for any security-sensitive use (signatures, password hashing, integrity over hostile data).
java-weak-crypto-md5.impact: An attacker can forge messages or files that share the same MD5 hash as a legitimate one, bypassing integrity or authentication checks.
java-weak-crypto-md5.fix: Use MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256") or stronger. For password hashing, use a slow KDF: BCrypt, PBKDF2, Argon2, or scrypt — never a raw hash.

java-weak-crypto-sha1.problem: SHA-1 is broken against collision attacks (SHAttered, 2017). It must not be used for digital signatures, certificate fingerprints, or any integrity check against an adversary.
java-weak-crypto-sha1.impact: Attackers can produce two different inputs that share the same SHA-1, bypassing signature or integrity verification.
java-weak-crypto-sha1.fix: Use SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-3 instead. For passwords, use BCrypt / Argon2 / PBKDF2.

java-weak-cipher-des.problem: DES uses a 56-bit key, which can be brute-forced in hours on modern hardware. It is obsolete and should never be used for confidentiality.
java-weak-cipher-des.impact: Any data encrypted with DES can be recovered by an attacker with modest resources.
java-weak-cipher-des.fix: Use AES with a strong mode: Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding") with a 128- or 256-bit random key and a unique 12-byte IV per message.

java-weak-cipher-ecb.problem: ECB encrypts each block independently, so identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks. Patterns in the plaintext leak through the ciphertext.
java-weak-cipher-ecb.impact: Attackers can detect repeated data, swap blocks between messages, or reconstruct parts of the plaintext.
java-weak-cipher-ecb.fix: Use an authenticated mode: AES/GCM/NoPadding with a unique IV per message. If you cannot use authenticated encryption, use AES/CBC/PKCS5Padding with a random IV plus a separate MAC (encrypt-then-MAC).

java-hardcoded-password.problem: A password, API key, or secret is written as a string literal in the source. Anyone with access to the repository, the compiled JAR, or a decompiler can read it.
java-hardcoded-password.impact: Total compromise of the account or service that secret protects. Rotating it requires a redeploy.
java-hardcoded-password.fix: Read secrets from environment variables, a configuration file outside the repo, or a secrets manager (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Spring Cloud Config with encrypted values).

java-jndi-lookup-user-input.problem: ctx.lookup() with a variable name lets the caller fetch arbitrary JNDI resources, including LDAP/RMI URLs that can return remote serialized objects executed by the JVM.
java-jndi-lookup-user-input.impact: Remote code execution — same class of bug as Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228).
java-jndi-lookup-user-input.fix: Never pass user input to lookup(). Use a fixed string for the JNDI name. Patch Log4j to a non-vulnerable version. Set com.sun.jndi.ldap.object.trustURLCodebase=false and com.sun.jndi.rmi.object.trustURLCodebase=false.

java-trust-all-x509.problem: An X509TrustManager with an empty checkServerTrusted accepts every certificate, including self-signed or expired ones, on every host.
java-trust-all-x509.impact: TLS no longer provides authentication — any attacker on the network path can present their own certificate and intercept traffic (MITM).
java-trust-all-x509.fix: Remove the custom TrustManager and use the JVM default (SSLContext.getDefault()). If you need to trust a private CA, install it in a custom KeyStore and pass that to TrustManagerFactory — never bypass validation entirely.

java-spring-permitall.problem: Spring Security .permitAll() makes a route reachable without authentication. It is correct for /login and static assets, but very dangerous on admin or API endpoints.
java-spring-permitall.impact: Anyone on the internet can call the endpoint as if they were authenticated — full data exposure or destructive actions, depending on the route.
java-spring-permitall.fix: Use .authenticated() or .hasRole("ADMIN") for protected routes. Reserve .permitAll() for clearly public assets, and review every occurrence on a real audit.

java-printstacktrace-prod.problem: e.printStackTrace() writes the full stack trace to standard error. In production, traces often leak class names, file paths, library versions, and database structure.
java-printstacktrace-prod.impact: Information disclosure that helps attackers fingerprint your stack and find exploitable libraries. Also unhelpful for operations because there is no log correlation.
java-printstacktrace-prod.fix: Use a logger: log.error("context message", e). For client-facing errors, return a generic message and an opaque request ID; log the details server-side.

java-null-comparison-equals.problem: Calling .equals(null) on a reference that is itself null throws NullPointerException before the comparison is even evaluated.
java-null-comparison-equals.impact: Unexpected NPE at runtime — common cause of crashes in code that meant to ask 'is this value null?'.
java-null-comparison-equals.fix: Write the literal on the left: null == x; or use Objects.equals(x, null); or simply x == null.

java-string-compare-eq.problem: In Java, == on String references compares identity, not content. It only happens to work for interned literals and breaks as soon as one side comes from input, a database, or new String(...).
java-string-compare-eq.impact: Comparisons that look correct in tests start returning false in production, producing wrong control flow and silent bugs.
java-string-compare-eq.fix: Use a.equals(b) or, safer against null on either side, Objects.equals(a, b). For null-tolerant constant comparisons, use "literal".equals(value).

java-resource-not-closed.problem: Opening a FileInputStream outside a try-with-resources block leaves the file handle open if any exception is thrown before close() is called.
java-resource-not-closed.impact: File descriptors leak over time, eventually exhausting OS limits and breaking unrelated parts of the application.
java-resource-not-closed.fix: Wrap the resource in try-with-resources: try (FileInputStream fis = new FileInputStream(path)) { ... } — the JVM closes it automatically, even on exception.

java-empty-catch.problem: An empty catch block silently swallows an exception. The error is lost: nobody logs it, nobody handles it, control flow continues as if nothing happened.
java-empty-catch.impact: Bugs become invisible. Failures that should stop or alert the system instead lead to silently corrupted state.
java-empty-catch.fix: At minimum, log the exception: log.warn("context", e). If recovery is intentional, leave a comment explaining why. Never just catch and pass.

java-system-out-println-prod.problem: System.out.println bypasses your logging infrastructure: no log level, no timestamp, no correlation ID, no rotation, no structured output.
java-system-out-println-prod.impact: Useful operational signals are scattered and hard to query. In containerized environments they often vanish entirely.
java-system-out-println-prod.fix: Use SLF4J or java.util.logging: log.info("message"), log.debug(...), etc. Configure the logger via your framework so output is structured, level-filtered, and aggregated.

java-todo-comment.problem: TODO and FIXME comments mark deferred work directly in source. If they are not tracked elsewhere, they age silently and the original author often forgets.
java-todo-comment.impact: Unresolved TODOs accumulate into invisible technical debt — some hide missing validations or security checks.
java-todo-comment.fix: Either fix the issue now, or convert the TODO into a tracked ticket and reference its number in the comment (e.g. // TODO #123: ...). Delete TODOs that no longer apply.
